raw_case_text:
In January 2019, a 40-year-old male patient presented with bleeding per-rectum, fever, loss of appetite, weight loss, and stool incontinence of 7 months, associated with generalized body swelling of 2 months. He had a mass around his anus for 10 years, which he considered as hemorrhoids and was not treated medically. For this, he visited Gondar University Hospital and was admitted to the medical unit for 2 weeks. His diagnosis was rectal carcinoma with anal incontinence, and he was transferred to the surgical unit, and he was appointed for further diagnostic workup. However, he came later than the appointment he was given, and after his symptoms had worsened. On investigation, an abdominal CT scan showed a 4 cm long polypoid enhancing mass in the anorectal junction with adjacent nodular fat stranding in the mesorectum. There was minimal ascites, with bilateral pleural effusion. The conclusion was an anorectal mass, likely carcinoma, with ascites and bilateral pleural effusion. Serum albumin was 1.2 mg/dl, and an HIV test was negative.
With the suspicion of rectal carcinoma, a diverting loop sigmoid colostomy was carried out through a left lower quadrant incision, and an incisional biopsy was performed. Multiple samples were taken from the rectal mass, and a wedge resection biopsy from the anal ulceration was performed. A colostomy bag was left in situ, and the patient was admitted to the surgical ward.
While awaiting diagnosis, the patient developed hospital-acquired pneumonia and was initiated on intravenous ceftriaxone, intravenous metronidazole, and intravenous tramadol at the surgical ward.
On the 24th day postsurgery, his biopsy result arrived. Microscopic examination from both the anal ulcer and rectal mass showed lymphoplasmacytic cell infiltrates along with foamy macrophages stuffed with intracellular Leishmania amastigotes (Figures 1 and 2). No features of malignancy were seen in both tissue sections. Other organisms mimicking Leishmania amastigotes such as Histoplasma were excluded morphologically on histology. Therefore, a diagnosis of leishmaniasis was made, and the patient was transferred to the Leishmaniasis Research and Treatment Center (LRTC).
The photographic image of histopathology was not available for case 1.
Once leishmaniasis was confirmed, the patient was transferred from the surgical ward to LRTC. At presentation to LRTC, his general appearance was chronically sick-looking and emaciated. His blood pressure was low at 80/50 mmHg, and his weight was 42 kg; height was not measured as the patient could not stand; other vital signs were in the normal range. On abdominal examination, there was a fluid collection but no organomegaly, and a colostomy bag was present on the left lower quadrant of the abdomen.
Per-rectum examination showed a 6 by 3 cm indurated ulcerating mass surrounding the anus and a fungating circumferential rectal mass 8 cm above the proximal anal verge, with loss of anal tone.
He was started on AmBisome 5 mg/kg IV daily and once weekly for 8 doses. While hospitalized, he developed gastritis with intractable vomiting, after which he developed severe hypokalemia with a serum potassium level of 2.2 mmol/L and elevated creatinine level of 1.7 mg/dl. For this, he was started on potassium (KCL) IV infusion, IV omeprazole, and IV hydration. Though the perianal lesion was decreasing to 4 by 3 cm, his general condition worsened due to hypoalbuminemia and massive uncontrollable colostomy diarrhea, and the patient died 18 days after the leishmaniasis diagnosis.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 40-year-old male presented with bleeding per-rectum, fever, loss of appetite, weight loss, and fecal incontinence for 7 months, with generalized body swelling for 2 months.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient had a 10-year history of an untreated perianal mass presumed to be hemorrhoids. Seven months prior to presentation, he developed rectal bleeding, fever, anorexia, progressive weight loss, and stool incontinence, followed 2 months prior by generalized body edema. He was admitted to a hospital medical ward for 2 weeks with suspected rectal carcinoma and anal incontinence before transfer for surgical evaluation. Following a diverting sigmoid colostomy and biopsy, he developed hospital-acquired pneumonia treated with intravenous antibiotics.
subjective.past_medical_history: Ten-year history of an untreated perianal mass presumed to be hemorrhoids. No other prior medical history or travel documented.
subjective.review_of_systems: Reports fever, loss of appetite, weight loss, stool incontinence, and generalized body swelling.

objective.physical_examination: Chronically sick-looking and emaciated. Blood pressure: 80/50 mmHg, weight: 42 kg (height unmeasurable as patient could not stand); other vitals in normal range. Abdomen: fluid collection present, no organomegaly, colostomy bag present in the left lower quadrant. Per-rectum examination: 6 cm x 3 cm indurated ulcerating mass surrounding the anus, and a fungating circumferential rectal mass 8 cm above the proximal anal verge with loss of anal tone.
objective.routine_investigations: Serum albumin: 1.2 mg/dl; serum potassium: 2.2 mmol/L; serum creatinine: 1.7 mg/dl; HIV serology: negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Abdominal CT scan: 4 cm long polypoid enhancing mass in the anorectal junction with adjacent nodular fat stranding in the mesorectum, minimal ascites, and bilateral pleural effusion (suggestive of anorectal carcinoma). Surgical incisional biopsy of rectal mass and wedge resection of anal ulceration: lymphoplasmacytic cell infiltrates with foamy macrophages containing intracytoplasmic inclusions; no features of malignancy.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Confirmation: Microscopic examination of biopsies from both the anal ulcer and rectal mass revealed foamy macrophages stuffed with intracellular Leishmania amastigotes. Histoplasma and other mimics were morphologically excluded, and no features of malignancy were observed, confirming mucosal/cutaneous leishmaniasis. Management and Outcome: Treated initially with IV ceftriaxone, IV metronidazole, and IV tramadol for hospital-acquired pneumonia. Following leishmaniasis confirmation, transferred to the Leishmaniasis Research and Treatment Center and initiated on liposomal amphotericin B (AmBisome) 5 mg/kg IV daily and once weekly for 8 doses. Course was complicated by gastritis with intractable vomiting, acute kidney injury (creatinine 1.7 mg/dl), and severe hypokalemia (potassium 2.2 mmol/L), managed with IV potassium replacement, IV omeprazole, and IV hydration. Although the perianal mass decreased to 4 cm x 3 cm, the patient experienced worsening hypoalbuminemia and massive uncontrollable colostomy diarrhea, leading to death 18 days after leishmaniasis diagnosis.
